# ArtaPattern

> ArtaPattern is the independent software architecture and backend engineering practice of Hamed Rezaei, a software architect and senior .NET backend engineer with 12+ years of C#/.NET experience. Specialties: software architecture and system design, .NET modernization and backend reliability, MetaTrader MT4/MT5 server plugin development for forex brokers, and GIS/WebGIS software development. Remote, project-based collaboration in English. Contact: hamedrezaei.ez@gmail.com

Past work shown on the site is Hamed Rezaei's professional experience before founding ArtaPattern, not ArtaPattern client engagements.

## Specialties
- [MetaTrader Plugin Development for Forex Brokers](https://artapattern.com/services/metatrader-plugin-development/): Independent MetaTrader plugin developer for forex brokers: MT4/MT5 server plugins in C++, dealing desk and slippage logic, plugin licensing platforms and .NET broker backends.
- [GIS & WebGIS Software Development](https://artapattern.com/services/gis-software-development/): GIS software development with .NET, Python and Android: WebGIS applications, spatial queries in SQL Server and PostgreSQL, field apps with offline maps, and ArcGIS, ArcEngine and AutoCAD integrations.
- [Software Architecture & System Design Consulting](https://artapattern.com/services/software-architecture-consulting/): Independent software architecture consulting: system design for new products, boundaries and data ownership, documented architecture decisions and an implementation direction for your team.
- [Agent-Based Systems & AI Integration](https://artapattern.com/services/ai-agent-systems/): Architecture and backend engineering for agent-based AI systems: tool and API design, MCP servers, permissions and approval gates, audit trails, long-running operations and integration with .NET backends.
- [.NET Modernization & Backend Reliability](https://artapattern.com/services/dotnet-modernization/): Modernize existing .NET systems without rewriting everything: incremental .NET Framework to modern .NET migration, architecture review, SQL Server performance and backend reliability.

## Starting engagements
- System Design (Building something new?): For a new product or major capability, before serious development starts: clear system boundaries and an implementation direction.
- Architecture Review (Working around a difficult legacy system?): For a team with a running system, often on .NET, that is unsure about its structure or where to take it next: what to improve, what to keep, and where to start.
- Backend Reliability Assessment (Facing backend performance or reliability issues?): For slow responses, recurring errors or failing background processing, investigated before committing to a major rewrite.

## Engineering Notes
- [When Does a Software Idea Become Alive?](https://artapattern.com/insights/when-software-becomes-alive/) (2026-10-12): Start with the first meaningful scenario, enough architecture to reduce uncertainty, and room to evolve.
- [SSE vs. SignalR for Real-Time Log Monitoring](https://artapattern.com/insights/sse-vs-signalr-real-time-log-monitoring/) (2026-10-11): Server-Sent Events, separate command and event paths, and lifecycle isolation between workers, backend and browser.
- [Capability Is Not Authority: Who Decides What AI Agents May Do?](https://artapattern.com/insights/ai-agent-capability-vs-authority/) (2026-10-10): Probabilistic, deterministic and hybrid execution paths, and a governance plane that decides approvals independently of model reasoning.
- [AI Agents Can Write Production Code. Can They Prove It Works?](https://artapattern.com/insights/harness-engineering-verified-ai-code/) (2026-10-10): Harness engineering: explicit contracts, isolated environments, closed feedback loops and verification gates around coding agents.
- [AI Can Accelerate Implementation. It Cannot Define Your Business Rules.](https://artapattern.com/insights/ai-coding-agents-business-rules/) (2026-10-07): Specify intent, establish domain language and build verification in before delegating work to a coding agent.

## MetaTrader Plugin Development for Forex Brokers
MT4/MT5 server plugins in C++, plugin management and licensing platforms, and the .NET backends around them, designed and built by an engineer who has shipped them for a forex brokerage.

- MT4/MT5 server plugins in C++: Dealing desk behavior with configurable, broker-oriented slippage management; copy trading; alarm and monitoring plugins for broker operations.
- Plugin management and licensing platforms: A control plane that holds plugin configuration and licences centrally and keeps customer-side runtimes in sync through a desired-state model.
- Broker backends and integrations: .NET services, React administration, ABP-based broker CRM work, Hangfire background jobs and SQL reporting.
- Blockchain payment R&D: BSC/BEP-20 transaction-service R&D with Domain-Driven Design, and architecture review of an existing TRON payment system.

Boundary: Not trading strategies, signals, investment advice or financial regulation compliance.

Q: Do you build MT4 and MT5 server plugins?
A: Yes. I have designed and built C++ server-side plugins for MT4 and MT5, including a dealing desk plugin with configurable slippage management, a copy trader plugin and an alarm system for broker operations.
Q: Can you manage plugin configuration and licensing across many servers?
A: Yes. I architected and delivered a plugin management and licensing platform from concept to V1: a .NET control plane with React administration, where customer-side runtime components converge on a centrally recorded desired state.
Q: Can you integrate MetaTrader with our backend or CRM?
A: Yes. My broker work includes .NET backend services, an ABP-based broker CRM, Hangfire job troubleshooting and SQL reporting. I usually start with an Architecture Review or a Backend Reliability Assessment.
Q: Do you work with brokers remotely?
A: Yes. I work remotely and project-based, in English. Scope, timeline and terms are agreed in writing before work begins.
Q: Do you offer trading strategies or investment advice?
A: No. My focus is server-side plugins and broker backend systems, not trading strategies, signals or investment advice.

WebGIS applications, spatial data and map-based field tools that connect location data to real workflows, from an engineer who has built GIS software since 2006.

- WebGIS applications: Browser-based GIS for municipal services and emergency response, including damage and aid estimation and nearest-facility analysis.
- Spatial data and queries: Spatial queries and stored procedures in SQL Server, PostgreSQL synchronization, and property maps tied to business workflows.
- Field and mobile apps: Android and Kotlin apps with offline maps, tracking and photo or video capture; offline tile caching with MapProxy.
- Desktop GIS and CAD integrations: ArcGIS plugins with Oracle synchronization, ArcEngine vehicle tracking, and AutoCAD automation for land-parcel boundaries.

Boundary: Software engineering with spatial data, not surveying or cartographic production.

Q: Do you build WebGIS applications?
A: Yes. I have built and contributed to WebGIS applications for municipal platforms, emergency response and sales distribution, using ASP.NET, Django and PostgreSQL.
Q: Can you add maps and spatial queries to an existing .NET system?
A: Yes. On a municipal platform I optimized SQL Server spatial queries, stored procedures and triggers, and tied requests and cases to property maps.
Q: Do you build field apps that work offline?
A: Yes. I have built Android apps with offline maps for city data collection, and offline tile caching with MapProxy.
Q: Do you work with ArcGIS?
A: Yes. I have developed ArcGIS plugins synchronized with an Oracle database and ArcEngine-based Windows applications for vehicle tracking.

## Software Architecture & System Design Consulting
Design new systems and make clearer architectural decisions: boundaries, data ownership, documented trade-offs and an implementation direction your team can follow.

- System design for new products: Context and container views, module and service boundaries, main flows and quality attributes.
- Architecture Decision Records: Options compared, the choice, its trade-offs and what would make you revisit it.
- Backend and platform architecture: API structure, integrations, shared capabilities and service lifecycle for maintainable growth.
- Implementation direction: A first slice and an incremental plan, with hands-on engineering support if useful.

Boundary: Not UI/UX design or infrastructure provisioning.

Q: What do I receive from a System Design engagement?
A: System boundaries and main flows, architecture decisions written down with their trade-offs, and an initial implementation direction for your team.
Q: Do you only advise, or also build?
A: Both. I stay hands-on: I independently architected and delivered a MetaTrader plugin management platform from concept to V1.
Q: Which technologies do you work with?
A: Mainly C#/.NET, ASP.NET Core, EF Core, SQL Server and PostgreSQL, with DDD, CQRS, modular and distributed architectures.

## Agent-Based Systems & AI Integration
LLM agents become useful when they can act on real systems. I design the architecture and backend that let them do it safely: tools, permissions, approvals, audit trails and operations that survive failure.

- Agent architecture: Which decisions the agent makes, which tools it may call, how context flows, and where a human approves.
- Tool APIs and MCP servers: Narrow, well-typed tools over your existing systems, exposed through function calling or the Model Context Protocol.
- Guardrails and audit: Permissions per tool, approval gates for irreversible actions, and an audit trail of every call and outcome.
- Reliable operations: Long-running and retryable operations with status tracking, so a dropped connection or a failed step does not leave the system in an unknown state.
- Evaluation and observability: Test scenarios for agent behavior, tracing of tool calls, and metrics that show whether the agent is actually helping.
- Integration with .NET backends: Agents connected to ASP.NET Core services, SQL Server or PostgreSQL data, and background processing you already run.

Boundary: Not foundation-model training or machine-learning research.

Q: What does an agent-based system need beyond the model?
A: Well-defined tools over your systems, permission checks per tool, human approval for irreversible actions, idempotent and retryable operations, an audit trail, and evaluation. Those parts decide whether an agent is safe to use in production.
Q: Can AI agents work with our existing .NET backend?
A: Yes. The usual approach is to expose narrow tools over your existing services, through function calling or an MCP server, instead of giving the agent direct database access.
Q: Do you build MCP servers?
A: Yes. I design and build Model Context Protocol servers and tool APIs that let agents use your systems with explicit permissions and logging.
Q: Where should an agent project start?
A: With one meaningful scenario: a single task the agent completes end to end, with its tools, guardrails and failure handling in place. A System Design engagement covers that first scenario.
Q: Do you use AI in your own delivery?
A: Yes. I use AI coding agents across discovery, planning, test-driven implementation, review and regression verification, with an engineer reviewing changes before they merge.

## .NET Modernization & Backend Reliability
Improve existing .NET systems without rewriting everything: incremental migration from .NET Framework, less complexity, and backend performance and reliability problems investigated to their cause.

- Incremental .NET migration: .NET Framework to modern .NET, subsystem by subsystem, with shared data and integrations kept stable.
- Architecture review and refactoring: Where complexity comes from, which changes pay off first, and a staged path to get there.
- SQL Server performance: Stored procedures, triggers and spatial queries optimized where the time is actually spent.
- Backend reliability: Failing background jobs, slow APIs and unreliable integrations investigated before committing to a rewrite.

Boundary: Not 24/7 on-call support or managed operations.

Q: Do we have to rewrite our .NET Framework application?
A: Usually not. I prefer migrating subsystem by subsystem while the system stays in use, as I did for five related subsystems moving to .NET 7.
Q: Where does a modernization engagement start?
A: With an Architecture Review: issues ranked by impact, options including what to keep, and recommended next steps with a first slice.
Q: Can you help with slow SQL Server queries or failing background jobs?
A: Yes. A Backend Reliability Assessment investigates the problem, tests hypotheses and gives corrective actions in priority order.

## SSE vs. SignalR for Real-Time Log Monitoring (https://artapattern.com/insights/sse-vs-signalr-real-time-log-monitoring/)
For real-time log monitoring across remote .NET workers, I evaluated WebSockets, SignalR and Server-Sent Events. SSE was the transport, server push was the pattern, and decoupling was the goal.

Q: When should I choose SSE instead of SignalR?
A: When browser clients only need server-to-client updates and commands already travel over ordinary HTTP APIs. SSE is plain HTTP with the text/event-stream format. SignalR is a better fit when you need two-way messaging, hub-style method calls, groups or transport fallback managed for you.
Q: Can Server-Sent Events send an Authorization header?
A: The browser's built-in EventSource API cannot set custom headers. Common options are cookie-based authentication, or reading the stream with fetch and a ReadableStream, which allows headers and cancellation but makes parsing and reconnection your responsibility.
Q: Is SSE a reliable messaging system?
A: No. SSE is a streaming transport. Durability, replay of missed events and ordering guarantees have to be designed at the application level, for example with event ids, sequence numbers and a bounded replay buffer, or with a real message broker behind the stream.
Q: Does a browser disconnect stop the worker?
A: It shouldn't. In this design the operation, the worker's log collection and the browser stream have separate lifecycles, so a closed tab only ends that one stream.

## Capability Is Not Authority: Who Decides What AI Agents May Do? (https://artapattern.com/insights/ai-agent-capability-vs-authority/)
AI agents are getting better at doing the work. The harder question is who decides what they are allowed to do, and where explicit human approval stays necessary.

Q: What is the difference between an agent's capability and its authority?
A: Capability is what an agent can do with its model, tools and context. Authority is what it is permitted to do: which identity it acts under, what it may change, and which steps still need a human decision. Better capability doesn't grant more authority on its own.
Q: What is an Agentic Development Platform (ADP)?
A: It's the direction I see for extending Internal Developer Platforms and Golden Paths so that AI agents are first-class consumers: an agent harness for context, tools and isolated execution, and a governance plane for identities, permissions, gates and approvals.
Q: Should an AI agent be allowed to approve its own release?
A: In the workflows I design, no. An agent can prepare changes and gather evidence, and passing checks is necessary, but release authority sits with an explicit approval boundary enforced outside the model.
Q: What is a bounded retry budget?
A: A limit on how many times an agent may try to fix a failing check on its own. When the budget runs out, the work escalates to a person instead of looping indefinitely.

## AI Agents Can Write Production Code. Can They Prove It Works? (https://artapattern.com/insights/harness-engineering-verified-ai-code/)
Generating code with AI agents keeps getting easier. Establishing confidence in that code doesn't. That gap moved my focus from writing better prompts to engineering better environments around agents.

Q: What is harness engineering?
A: Designing the tools, context, constraints and feedback loops around an AI agent so it can work reliably: explicit contracts, decisions that persist between sessions, isolated environments, the ability to observe failures, and verification gates before production.
Q: How is harness engineering different from prompt engineering?
A: Prompting shapes a single instruction. A harness shapes the environment the agent works in, so behavior can be checked against evidence rather than assumed from the instruction.
Q: What is a Last Known Good configuration?
A: The most recent configuration a component validated and stored locally. If the backend becomes unavailable, the component can keep running on it safely instead of failing or running unconfigured.
Q: How can an AI agent verify its own changes?
A: By working in an environment where it can run tests, reproduce failure scenarios such as an unavailable dependency, read the resulting logs and state, and submit changes through defined gates, rather than declaring success from the code alone.

## AI Can Accelerate Implementation. It Cannot Define Your Business Rules. (https://artapattern.com/insights/ai-coding-agents-business-rules/)
A coding agent can implement license validation in minutes. It cannot decide what should happen when a license expires. That decision is a business policy with architectural consequences.

Q: Can an AI coding agent decide business rules?
A: It will often fill gaps with plausible defaults, but those are guesses. Rules such as expiry behavior, offline use or renewal timing are business policies. Someone accountable for the domain has to decide them and make them explicit.
Q: What should a specification for a coding agent include?
A: Expected behavior, constraints, system boundaries and acceptance criteria, including failure scenarios. A task description says what to work on; a specification says what a correct result must do.
Q: Why does DDD's Ubiquitous Language matter for AI-assisted development?
A: Terms like active subscription, valid license and authorized runtime can mean different things in different bounded contexts. Making those distinctions explicit helps people and agents implement the same rule.
Q: Is passing tests enough to accept code written by an agent?
A: Passing tests are evidence, not proof. If the tests were written from the same misunderstanding as the code, both will agree and still be wrong. Domain clarification, review and regression checks close that gap.
